As I recall it from SCOPe, and without a live lookup, all three are in class b (all-beta), in the Cupredoxin-like fold (b.6) and the Cupredoxins superfamily (b.6.1). Plastocyanin/azurin-like proteins are the family b.6.1.1. The ephrin ectodomain and the PAD4 N-terminal domain are, as I recall, classified in separate families of that superfamily. I am not certain of their exact family-level sccs numbers or of the release-specific entries, so check those against the SCOPe release you are using. Being in one superfamily means SCOPe judges them to share a common evolutionary origin. That judgment rests on the shared Greek-key beta-sandwich/barrel topology plus structural and functional features. It does not rest on sequence similarity. The different families show that the relationship is distant. The proteins are unrelated at the family level, share little or no detectable sequence identity, and have diverged a great deal in function. So the apparent biological unrelatedness is real at the functional level. It does not contradict the structural classification, because superfamily membership records fold-level descent, not shared activity.

Copper binding and electron transfer should not be inferred across them. Those properties belong to the plastocyanin/azurin-like family. They depend on a specific set of copper ligands, typically His, Cys, His and a axial Met, held in a loop at one end of the barrel. Ephrin ectodomains are Eph-receptor-binding ligands. They act in cell-cell signalling and need no metal. PAD4 is a calcium-dependent peptidylarginine deiminase. Its N-terminal domain is a regulatory/structural domain of that enzyme, and calcium, not copper, is relevant to PAD4. A shared fold does not carry a ligand site or a redox role. To claim copper binding or electron transfer for any of these proteins you would need conserved ligand residues in an alignment or structure superposition, direct metal-binding evidence, and redox or electron-transfer measurements. Without that evidence, the classification supports only a shared structural scaffold and ancient homology. It does not support predicting metal binding, redox activity, or function from one of these proteins to another. It is also a weak basis for choosing one as a template for another's active site or interface.
